newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen comfortable with new Clinton team.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen comfortable with new Clinton team.

text.p: Wall Street is comfortable with the fresh string of Cabinet nominations President Clinton made on Friday, according to some of the financial community's more prominent figures.
For Wall Street, the most significant, although the least surprising, of these was the renomination of Robert Rubin to continue as U.S. Treasury Secretary.
"That was the key one; no one was surprised by it," said David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co., a primary dealer of U.S. government securities.
The president made his announcements at an afternoon news conference.
"Financial markets have a very high opinion of Rubin and see him as the anchor of Clinton's economic team," said Jones.
Rubin was co-chairman of Goldman Sachs & Co. before going to Washington D.C. to work for Clinton.
Clinton also retained Lawrence Summers as Deputy Treasury Secretary and Franklin Raines as budget director.
Clinton nominated acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky to permanent status in that post. She would succeed Mickey Kantor who is returning to private life.
The Barshevksy appointment drew praise from Allen Sinai, chief executive officer and chief global economist of Primark Decision Economics.

"Barshevsky is a very positive appointment," said Sinai. "She will continue what has been a very successful trade policy -- a policy that is a mixture of free trade and, where appropriate, hand-to-hand combat.

"Free trade has to be bi-lateral," said Sinai. "Both trading partners have to be practicing it. The tough hand-to-hand combat approach that (Mickey) Kantor took was appropriate and Barshefsky is in that mold.
Clinton's naming of Gene Sperling to direct the National Economic Council also drew plaudits from Sinai -- "Sperling is an excellent choice" -- and faint praise from Jones.
"As far as I know, he's very liberal," said Jones. "He probably got the job because he's been with Clinton for some time."
Jones said the effectiveness of the National Economic Council is very sensitive to the strength of the person who runs it.
"It was effective when Rubin was the head of it," said Jones. "The person who runs it must have the President's ear."

The nomination of William Daley as Commerce Secretary aroused scant interest on Wall Street. Daley, the brother of Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, is the lawyer who spearheaded the White House drive to push the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) through Congress.
Clinton also asked Janet Reno to remain as his Attorney General and Carol Browner to remain as EPA Administrator. He nominated Rep. Bill Richardson as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations.
"There are no surprises," said Jones. "It's very much the same idea as the election. 'Don't rock the boat' is the name of the game in Washington. Changes will be incremental."
